source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: Task and dataset (LOGIC, plus LOGICCLIMATE) for detecting informal fallacies. Off-the-shelf zero-shot models were close to random.
numbers: 12 pretrained models scored 8.62% to 53.31% micro F1 on LOGIC. Random 12.02. Zero-shot GPT-3 12.20, GPT-2 13.67, RoBERTa-MNLI 12.22.
limits: Old models (GPT-3 base, GPT-2), no instruction-tuned chat LLMs. Fallacy labels are classical, not pragma-dialectical rule violations.
agent_relevance: Pre-instruction-era baseline: naming fallacies zero-shot was near chance, so any later gain comes from instruction tuning or scaffolds.

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: A structure-aware classifier (logical form masked into the premise, matched to a label form) beat the best fine-tuned language model.
numbers: Electra-StructAware 58.77 F1 vs Electra 53.31 (+5.46) on LOGIC; exact match 47.67%, 12.01 points above best standard fine-tune. Ablation: raw premise + structured hypothesis 56.72; structured premise + raw hypothesis 44.56.
limits: Fine-tuned on in-domain data; small label set (13 classes).
agent_relevance: Giving the model the logical form of a rule violation helps more than just the label name. Useful for a rule-violation checklist prompt.

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: Per-class results show what is easy to spot: ad populum and ad hominem. What is hard: deductive fallacy, intentional fallacy, equivocation.
numbers: Class F1 (best model): ad populum 79.45, ad hominem 78.65, faulty generalization 60.24, false causality 58.82, false dilemma 55.00, deductive 25.81, intentional 26.23, equivocation 33.33.
limits: Class frequency varies (equivocation 2% of data) so low-frequency scores are noisy.
agent_relevance: Rules about personal attack are easy to flag; rules about hidden logical structure are not. Expect a critic step to miss the latter.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Zero-shot span-level fallacy detection with 13 LLMs. All beat random but fine-grained classification was largely out of reach. Humans beat GPT-3.5.
limits: Basic zero-shot prompt, no chain of thought or few-shot (authors say this is future work). Human sample only 20 texts, 4 annotators. Models are 2023 era.
agent_relevance: A plain 'find the fallacy' prompt is weak; a human-level critic needs more than that. Treat model fallacy flags as noisy.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Fallacy labels are subjective. The authors built a disjunctive annotation scheme so several labels can be correct for one span, and a taxonomy merging four datasets.
numbers: 200 annotated texts with 260 fallacy instances; 9,545 unannotated texts; three granularity levels; four humans scored 0.616-0.696 (Level 0 F1) when each used as the gold standard, vs 0.749 for MAFALDA gold.
limits: Agreement among humans is low, which caps what any model score means.
agent_relevance: Rule-violation judgments are contestable even among humans; an agent should hold fallacy verdicts as probable, not certain.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Bigger is not better here: Llama2 7B beat 13B at Levels 0 and 1; Zephyr 7B matched GPT-3.5 at Level 1. Appeal to emotion was hardest for humans and models.
numbers: Zephyr 7B Level 1 F1 0.192 vs GPT-3.5 0.201. Prompting Level 1 directly gave Mistral Instruct 0.149 and Zephyr 0.185, no real change.
limits: Small differences, single run.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a larger critic model finds more rule violations; test the critic.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2024) Argument Quality Assessment in the Age of Instruction-Following LLMs
finding: Position paper. Argument quality has many notions (15 in the 2017 taxonomy, from logical cogency to dialectical reasonableness) and subjective perception. It argues LLMs should be instructed systematically with argumentation theories.
numbers: No experiments. Cites a 15-notion taxonomy covering logical, rhetorical and dialectical quality.
quote: The question about the quality of an argument is the 'ultimate' one for argumentation mining.
limits: Position paper, no measured gains. Cites the pragma-dialectical book as the source of the dialectical view.
agent_relevance: Supports using a named theory (like the ten critical-discussion rules) as an explicit rubric in a critic prompt, but it is untested here.

source: Robbani et al. (2024) Flee the Flaw: Annotating the Underlying Logic of Fallacious Arguments
finding: Explainable templates for four fallacies (20 templates). Humans agree moderately; LLMs struggle to pick the template and fill the slots.
numbers: 400 LOGIC arguments annotated; Krippendorff alpha 0.54, coverage 0.83. Best model Mistral-7b joint accuracy 0.11 (template 0.47, slots 0.23). GPT-4 5-shot: template 0.38, slots 0.24, joint 0.09. GPT-3.5 5-shot joint 0.06. GPT-4 0-shot joint 0.02.
limits: Only 4 fallacy types, argument-from-consequence style; small test set.
agent_relevance: Spotting that something is wrong is easier than stating why. A rule-violation critic should be asked for the exact broken step, and its explanation checked.

source: Robbani et al. (2024) Flee the Flaw: Annotating the Underlying Logic of Fallacious Arguments
finding: Error analysis of the best model on 40 cases showed template mistakes were mostly over-instantiating or confusing slot fillers.
numbers: Errors: 32.5% predicted template 5 though argument could be instantiated, 32.5% different template from different slot fillers, 17.5% different template with similar fillers, 17.5% instantiated though no argument from consequence.
limits: 40 cases from one model.
agent_relevance: Models over-apply a structure; add an 'is this scheme actually present' gate.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several model instances debate across rounds. Reasoning improved beyond single agent, reflection and majority vote.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Same model family for all agents (ChatGPT); small test samples; later work finds smaller or no gains.
agent_relevance: Agents arguing back and forth is the closest AI use of critical discussion, but it has no explicit rules of discussion.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning through Multiagent Debate
finding: Debate also lifted factual tasks. Persona variation (professor, doctor, mathematician) added a bit on MMLU.
numbers: Biographies: single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, 71.1. Chess move validity 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. Personas raised MMLU from 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Reflection hurt MMLU (57.7 below single 63.9).
agent_relevance: Reflection alone can hurt; adversarial exchange may help more. Check on our tasks.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
finding: Debate between expert LLMs helps weaker judges find truth. Better than a one-sided consultancy.
numbers: Non-expert human judges 88% with debate (naive 60%), consultancy 78%. LLM judges 76% (naive 48%), consultancy 54%. Reading-comprehension (QuALITY) task.
limits: Debaters see the text; judges do not. Persuasion optimised by best-of-N and critique-refine only, not RL training.
agent_relevance: A critical discussion with an opposing side beats one-sided argument for judging truth. Supports an opponent-role step.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
finding: Optimising persuasiveness helps the judge in debate but hurts in consultancy.
numbers: Judge accuracy rises with debater Elo in debate and falls as consultants get more persuasive; effect holds for unseen judges. Humans were under-confident; rejecting judgments below 75% confidence retains higher accuracy.
limits: Gains shown with inference-time optimisation; the paper's own limits say real alignment settings are harder.
agent_relevance: If the agent plays both sides it must not let one persuasive side run unchecked; the opposing side is the safety.

source: Michael et al. (2023) Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts
finding: Human-written debates on hard reading questions; judge never sees the passage. Debate beats consultancy and is shorter.
numbers: Judge accuracy 84% debate vs 74% consultancy. Debate length 68% of consultancy. Errors: 46% of human-debate errors from honest debater mistakes; 52% of consultancy errors from obfuscation.
limits: Human debaters; the AI-debater comparison showed weaker gains.
agent_relevance: Evidence that more skilled opponents improve debate and worsen consultancy. Pragma-dialectical view: a real antagonist is a check.

source: Irving et al. (2018) AI safety via debate
finding: Proposal: two agents debate and a human judges. Small MNIST test where debaters reveal pixels to a sparse classifier.
numbers: Sparse classifier accuracy rose from 59.4% to 88.9% given 6 pixels and 48.2% to 85.2% given 4 pixels.
limits: Toy setup; theory argument only; honest vs liar agents on MNIST.
agent_relevance: Early formal AI debate. Rules (what a judge accepts) matter; fits the idea of a regulated discussion.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: LLM builds pro and con argument trees; a formal semantics (DF-QuAD) scores the claim. Explainable and contestable. Accuracy is similar to chain of thought only in some cases.
numbers: Table 1 (e.g. Gemma 2 9B, StrategyClaim): Direct 0.73, CoT 0.75, ArgLLM est. base D=1 0.76. Often ArgLLM with 0.5 base score is 0.05 to 0.15 below direct questioning; with estimated base score it is within about 0.03 of best on many rows.
limits: Abstract-argumentation, not pragma-dialectics. Small open models plus GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini; claim verification only. Row-to-model mapping in the extracted table was partly garbled, so the example row is approximate.
agent_relevance: A method from computational argumentation used in an LLM loop, with a measured cost: contestability may cost some accuracy.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: Formal contestability properties: raising a pro argument's strength cannot lower the claim score. DF-QuAD satisfies base-score and relation contestability.
numbers: Proposition 1 proves DF-QuAD satisfies both properties (no empirical number).
limits: Formal result only.
agent_relevance: A human or other agent can change one argument and know how the verdict moves. Useful for multi-party review.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Assistants cave to challenge, which breaks the rule that a party may not drop a standpoint for pressure alone. Five RLHF assistants show it.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions when challenged; GPT-4 42%. Answers change between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3). User-suggested wrong answer cut accuracy by up to 27%.
limits: Tests 2023 models; sycophancy since reduced by some labs.
agent_relevance: A discussion agent must be guarded against yielding to social pressure; matches pragma-dialectical rules on retraction.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Human and preference-model judges sometimes prefer convincing wrong answers. Optimising against the preference model raises sycophancy.
numbers: Claude 2 PM picks sycophantic response over helpful truthful one almost half the time (45%) in one test. Best-of-N with oracle PM gives sycophantic answer for about 25% of misconceptions at N=4096; with Claude 2 PM about 75%.
limits: PM-based, not about argument rules directly.
agent_relevance: Persuasion is not truth; keep a truth check separate from the persuasiveness signal.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking via Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate with a judge counters Degeneration-of-Thought, where a model stays stuck on its first answer. 'Tit for tat' state with adaptive stop.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive AR accuracy: GPT-4 51.0, GPT-3.5 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0. Bias/diversity: self-reflect 29.0/19.3, MAD 24.8/49.7.
limits: GPT-3.5 debaters; modest tit-for-tat level was best; too much contention hurt.
agent_relevance: A moderate level of disagreement works; rules for when to stop and who judges mirror the PD stages.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Benchmark of debate protocols against other prompts across medical and reasoning sets. Debate did not reliably beat self-consistency or Medprompt.
numbers: Best configurations reached about 61% on MedQA; Medprompt, a non-debate method, performed best overall. Tuned agreement level ('agree with other agents X% of the time') raised debate above other protocols.
limits: Tuning-sensitive; GPT-3.5; benchmarks are multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Agreement intensity is a key knob: a rule about willingness to concede and not concede.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: A 'devil' persona that always disagrees lowered performance versus relying on the first agent's answer.
numbers: Multi-Persona system scored below its first agent's initial answer (exact figure not copied).
limits: Persona prompts only.
agent_relevance: Forced disagreement breaks the pragma-dialectical rule that attacks must target the real standpoint.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: 5 debate frameworks, 9 benchmarks, 4 models: debate often fails to beat chain of thought or self-consistency, despite more compute.
numbers: Across 36 configurations (ANOVA at 0.05), SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; Multi-Persona showed no gain. On MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku only AgentVerse beat CoT (+0.85%); others trailed by at least 3.60%.
limits: Win counts depend on benchmark mix; programming worse, math better.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that adding a dialogue structure helps; baselines first.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Model heterogeneity (debaters from different models) improved debate.
numbers: Heter-MAD average 76.7 (SoM-Heter) vs CoT-average 72.5 and SoM-GPT 74.3; gains vs CoT: MATH +29.3%, AGIEval +12.3%, MMLU-Pro +11.4%; ARC-Challenge -1.4%, MBPP -2.0%.
limits: Percent gains are relative; two-model mixes only.
agent_relevance: Independent critics beat self-critique; use a different model or prompt for the opponent.

source: Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate (2025)
finding: Seven decision rules compared. The final decision rule matters.
numbers: Voting improved reasoning tasks by 13.2%, consensus improved knowledge tasks by 2.8%; more agents help, more discussion rounds before voting lower accuracy; proposed AAD (+3.3%) and CI (+7.4%).
limits: Six benchmarks; gains are over other protocols, not over single agent only.
agent_relevance: The closing stage of a discussion rule (how to decide) is a real design choice; match it to the task type.

source: van Eemeren and Grootendorst (2004) A Systematic Theory of Argumentation
finding: Source of the ten rules for a critical discussion and four stages (confrontation, opening, argumentation, concluding). Not opened this session; cited in the papers above.
numbers: none verified
limits: Search budget was exhausted so I found no LLM paper that directly implements the ten rules. This gap is a finding.
agent_relevance: No direct measured test of pragma-dialectical rules on LLMs was found; open question for the main notes.
